subject: Cognitive Science
title: How We See Color
description: A quick, practical guide to How We See Color.

hook.text: A red apple isn't red. It absorbs every wavelength except red, which it bounces back to your eyes.

buildup.text: Three types of cone cells in your retina respond to short (blue), medium (green), and long (red) wavelengths.

discovery.text: Color is a mix ratio. Yellow isn't a wavelength between red and green—it's your brain blending both signals.

twist.text: Colors that don't exist on the spectrum—like magenta—are invented by your brain. No single wavelength makes magenta.

climax.text: Color vision is a compression algorithm. The brain reduces millions of wavelength combos into a manageable handful.

punchline.text: Color isn't in the world—it's in your brain.

quiz.question: How many types of cone cells do humans have?

details.summary: Color vision starts with three types of cone cells in the retina, each sensitive to different light wavelengths. But color is far more than receptor activity. The brain compares signals across cones, applies context corrections, and constructs the vivid color experience entirely internally.
details.whyItMatters: Color feels objective but is entirely constructed by the brain. Understanding this explains color illusions, color blindness, and why colors look different in different lighting.
takeaways: Three cone types detect short, medium, and long wavelengths
The brain constructs color by comparing signals across cones
Color perception is heavily influenced by surrounding context

faq.question: Why do colors look different in different lighting?
faq.answer: Your brain tries to compute the true color of an object regardless of illumination, a process called color constancy. It mostly succeeds, but when lighting is ambiguous, the system can be tricked. The famous blue-and-black versus white-and-gold dress illusion exploited this ambiguity.

faq.question: Do other animals see colors we cannot?
faq.answer: Yes. Many birds and insects have four types of color receptors, including ultraviolet sensitivity. Mantis shrimp have 16 types. Some animals see fewer colors. Human trichromatic vision is just one solution. The colors we experience are not properties of the world but of our specific visual system.
